title: Weakness upon weakness
hookLine: his mother carried him in weakness upon weakness, so thank Me and your parents (31:14)

cards: The last weeks of a pregnancy. The back that aches whatever you do. Sleeping propped on pillows, getting up again and again in the night.
Then the birth. Then the newborn months, feeding through the night on almost no sleep while the body is still recovering.
In the middle of Luqman's advice to his son, the Qur'an interrupts, in God's own voice, to say something about exactly that.

teach.b: Luqman has just told his son not to ascribe partners to God. Then come two verses that aren't Luqman's; they're God speaking. We have enjoined on the human being concerning his parents.
Pickthall: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years". Then: give thanks to Me and to your parents; to Me is the journey's end.
Weakness upon weakness, wahnan 'ala wahn. Commentators read it as weakness piled on weakness: the strain of pregnancy getting heavier month by month, then birth, then nursing. The verse sees it.
Notice the order of thanks: to Me, and to your parents. In one breath, gratitude to God and to the people who carried and raised you are joined. Then the next verse adds a limit.
If your parents strive to make you associate with God what you have no knowledge of, don't obey them; and yet keep company with them in this world kindly.

Even in disagreement about the most important thing, the kindness stays. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ underlined the mother's place. In a hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, a man asks who most deserves his good company.
Your mother, the Prophet says. Then who? Your mother.
Then who? Your mother. Then who?
Your father. Some commentators connect the threefold mother to three hardships: carrying, birth, nursing. Not every relationship with a mother is easy, and the verse doesn't say it is.
What it asks is that people remember what was carried.

how: Muslims treat kindness to parents, birr al-walidayn, as a major duty that follows directly after the worship of God, and pray for their parents, living or dead.

o: the two years before a child is weaned
weakness, the strain a mother carries
the pain of childbirth alone, nothing more

games.q: weakness upon weakness — tap the pairs.

s: 31:14 is Luqman speaking to his son
it's God's voice, interrupting Luqman's advice.
the next verse says to obey parents even in shirk
it says don't obey them in that, but keep company with them kindly.
in the hadith, the mother is named three times before the father

games.q: your parents are pushing you to put something in God's place. you won't. what do the verses say about how you treat them?
o: don't obey in that, but keep company with them kindly.
games.why: 31:15: if they strive to make you associate partners with God, don't obey them, yet keep company with them in this world kindly.

practice: Think of your mother, or whoever mothered you: a grandmother, an aunt, a foster parent, an older sister, and find one specific thing she carried for you that you probably never thanked her for, a night shift, a school run, a meal she skipped.
If she's gone, or things are complicated, you can simply hold her in mind kindly. If you pray, you can pray for her.

wordCard.voice: Wahn. Weakness, the Qur'an's word for what a mother carries, doubled as wahnan 'ala wahn, weakness upon weakness: pregnancy, birth and nursing, strain piled on strain. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: weakness upon weakness, the mother's burden in 31:14.

carryVoice: Your line: remember what was carried. Kindness stays, even where things are hard. See you tomorrow.
